# spatialkit

<!-- badges: start -->
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/spatialkit)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=spatialkit)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

spatialkit draws analysis regions, which it calls cells, from where your
observations are, instead of borrowing boundaries drawn for other purposes,
and summarises point data onto them with a count, a standard error and a
pooled value for every cell. It then scores regression models on
cross-validation folds that hold out whole blocks of space, and marks where a
fitted map extrapolates.

## The problem this solves

You have observations at points and need values over areas. The usual move is
to borrow boundaries that already exist: ZIP code areas, census tracts,
counties, sales territories. They were drawn for mail delivery, enumeration or
politics, so part of any answer aggregated onto them comes from the
partition. This is the modifiable areal
unit problem: the same observations, aggregated under different boundaries,
can give different conclusions.

spatialkit draws the cells from the data, in three steps:

1. Pick a cell count. `resolution_profile()` and `select_resolution()` set it
   from a size of 4.5 observations per cell by default, and report the
   leave-one-out error of the cell values. Given a ladder of counts, the
   profile scores each one against the spatial structure of the observations.
2. Place the cells. `get_voronoi_seeds()` places seeds by density-weighted
   k-means, so cells are small where observations are dense, and
   `build_tessellation()` grows Voronoi cells from them (or lays hex or square
   cells, or Delaunay triangles), clipped to your study area.
   `build_tessellation()` numbers the cells from their geometry, so the same
   seeds in a different row order give the same cell IDs.
3. Summarise. `summarize_by_cell()` gives each cell a count, a mean with its
   standard error, and a pooled value: the cell's mean pulled toward the mean
   of the observations in the 8 nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their
   observations). When the cell means stand in for a population mean, it can
   correct the standard errors for autocorrelation within the cells, which on
   a correlated field can double them or more.

The first figure shows a simulated field on 280 random sites in North
Carolina, aggregated onto three kinds of cells, about 30 of each: Voronoi
cells from density-weighted seeds, a hex grid and a square grid.

![Four maps of North Carolina: a simulated field at 280 sites, and its cell means on 30 Voronoi cells from density-weighted seeds, on a hex grid and on a square grid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/main/man/figures/readme-tessellations.png)\ 

The next figure cuts the same field at three cell counts, each cell showing its
pooled value. `resolution_profile()` scores each count by the leave-one-out
error of the pooled values at that count. The error is 0.33 at 12 cells, 0.18
at 62 cells (the count the default size of 4.5 observations per cell gives)
and 0.18 at 140 cells (two per cell). The 12 cells blur the hotspot in the
east. At 140 cells the error is within one standard error of the default's.
`vignette("resolution")` covers how the count is chosen.

![Four maps of North Carolina: the simulated field at 280 sites, and its pooled cell values at 12, 62 and 140 Voronoi cells, where 62 is the default count](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/main/man/figures/readme-resolution.png)\ 

The second half of the package tests the result. Three model backends (random
forest, GWR and a Bayesian GP) sit behind one `spatial_fit` class, so they can
be scored on the same folds. Cross-validation holds out whole blocks, of a
grid by default, which can be sized from the data's own autocorrelation range
or matched to the locations a map will predict at. An area-of-applicability
estimate marks where the resulting score applies. All of it is built on
[`sf`](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/), and each function that measures a
distance moves a lon/lat layer into a projected CRS first.

Random folds put a test point's neighbours in the training set, so a model
that can memorise location is scored on points it has nearly seen. Block folds
hold out whole blocks instead; the quick start below shows the difference in
RMSE.

![Two maps of North Carolina: 280 sites coloured by fold, mixed at random on the left and grouped into spatial blocks on the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/main/man/figures/readme-spatial-cv.png)\ 

## Scope

- **Regression, with one exception.** `fit_rf_model()` and `fit_gwr_model()`
  fit a numeric response and refuse a logical, factor or character one;
  `fit_gwr_model()` also refuses an integer-coded two-valued response and
  points to `GWmodel::ggwr.basic()`. The exception is
  `fit_bayesian_spatial_model()`, which also fits a binary response under
  `brms::bernoulli()`, and a factor or character response under
  `brms::categorical()` or an ordinal family. `cv_bayes()`
  refuses the categorical and ordinal families, because it scores one predicted
  number per row.
- **Vector data only.** There is no raster input or output: `predict_surface()`
  returns an `sf` POINT layer, which you convert yourself if you need a
  `SpatRaster`. The models work on points: `prep_model_data()` and
  `coerce_to_points()` reduce lines and polygons to points.
- **No areal or lattice models.** Moran's I here tests residuals for spatial
  structure. There is no CAR, SAR or spatial-lag fitter.
- **No spatio-temporal folds.** Every fold scheme is spatial; none holds out
  time.

## Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("spatialkit")
```

The development version installs from GitHub:

```{r install-dev, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit")
```

`sf`, `dplyr`, `logger`, `digest` and `FNN` install with it. Optional packages
switch on the model backends, variograms and plots;
[Get started](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/getting-started.html)
lists which does what. If you are upgrading from 2.0.0, the
[changelog](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/news/index.html)
lists the defaults that change results and the argument that restores each.

## Quick start

A simulated field of 400 observations in a 1,000 m square, with one weak
measured predictor `w`:

```{r quick-fixture}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(42)
n  <- 400
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$w <- rnorm(n)
# Mostly a smooth spatial field (exponential, effective range 3 x 80 = 240 m),
# with the weak predictor on top.
xy$z <- 0.5 * xy$w +
  as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 80) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
  rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
site <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
```

Set the cell count, draw Voronoi cells from the data and summarise onto them:

```{r quick-cells}
size <- select_resolution(resolution_profile(site, "z"))
size

seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(n = size, sample_points = site)
tess  <- build_tessellation(seeds,
                            boundary = clip_target_for(site, quiet = TRUE),
                            method = "voronoi", quiet = TRUE)
asg   <- assign_features_to_polygons(site, tess$cells,
                                     polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
cells <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = tess$cells)

head(st_drop_geometry(cells)[, c("cell_id", "n", "resp_mean_z", "..se_resp_z",
                                 "..pooled_resp_z")], 4)
```

```{r quick-kish, include=FALSE}
kish <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = tess$cells,
                          deff = "kish")
kish_ratio <- median(kish$..se_resp_z / cells$..se_resp_z, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The default size gives `r size$best` cells, each holding between
`r min(cells$n)` and `r max(cells$n)` observations. Each row has a count, the
cell mean, its standard error and the pooled value `..pooled_resp_z`, the
cell's mean pulled toward its neighbours by a weight that grows with the cell's
count (`?summarize_by_cell`, "Pooled values"). That standard error is the one
for the cell's own mean when its points are spread through the cell. When the
cell means stand in for the population mean, `deff = "kish"` widens each
standard error for the correlation inside the cell; on these cells it
multiplies them by `r format(round(kish_ratio, 1), nsmall = 1)` (median).
`?summarize_by_cell` says which to use when.

Then score a model. A random forest given the coordinates
(`include_coords = TRUE`) can fit the training surface by memorising location.
Score it on random folds and on blocks of at least 250 m, just above the
field's effective range (this needs `ranger`):

```{r quick-cv, eval=has_ranger}
fr <- make_folds(site, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fb <- make_folds(site, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 250,
                 seed = 1)

random  <- cv_rf(site, "z", "w", folds = fr, include_coords = TRUE)
blocked <- cv_rf(site, "z", "w", folds = fb, include_coords = TRUE)

c(random = random$overall$RMSE, blocked = blocked$overall$RMSE)
```

```{r quick-cv-text, echo=FALSE, results="asis", eval=has_ranger}
rmse <- function(cv) format(round(cv$overall$RMSE, 2), nsmall = 2)
cat("On the same 400 observations and the same model, random folds give an",
    "RMSE of", rmse(random), "and the blocks, built",
    round(fb$params$block_width), "m wide, give", paste0(rmse(blocked), "."),
    "The data and the model are the same; the random figure is the error of",
    "predicting among the samples, and the blocked one the error of predicting",
    "into gaps a block wide.")
```
A map's error depends on where it predicts, and
`fold_separation()` compares the folds' distances from the training data with
the map's. On real data the range is estimated, by `estimate_sac_range()` or
`make_folds(auto_range = TRUE)`; `vignette("spatial-cross-validation")` covers
that choice.

## The pipeline

Steps 1 to 10 link to their section of the
[reference index](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html),
and every step to the article that shows it. `?spatialkit` lists the same
steps inside R.

| Step | Main functions | Article |
|---|---|---|
| 1. [Prepare the data](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#prepare-the-data) | `ensure_projected()`, `coerce_to_points()`, `prep_model_data()` | [Get started](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/getting-started.html) |
| 2. [Measure spatial autocorrelation](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#measure-spatial-autocorrelation) | `estimate_sac_range()` | [Spatial cross-validation](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/spatial-cross-validation.html) |
| 3. [Choose a resolution](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#choose-a-resolution) | `resolution_profile()`, `select_resolution()` | [Choosing a resolution](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/resolution.html) |
| 4. [Build the cells](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#build-the-cells) | `get_voronoi_seeds()`, `build_tessellation()` | [Building cells and summarising them](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/cells.html) |
| 5. [Assign and summarise](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#assign-and-summarise) | `assign_features_to_polygons()`, `summarize_by_cell()` | [Building cells and summarising them](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/cells.html) |
| 6. [Make folds](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#make-folds) | `make_folds()`, `fold_separation()` | [Spatial cross-validation](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/spatial-cross-validation.html) |
| 7. [Fit a model](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#fit-a-model) | `fit_rf_model()`, `fit_gwr_model()`, `fit_bayesian_spatial_model()` | [Fitting and checking models](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/models.html) |
| 8. [Cross-validate and compare](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#cross-validate-and-compare) | `cv_rf()`, `cv_gwr()`, `cv_bayes()`, `compare_models_cv()` | [Spatial cross-validation](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/spatial-cross-validation.html) |
| 9. [Choose predictors](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#choose-predictors) | `select_features_forward()` | [Fitting and checking models](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/models.html) |
| 10. [Predict a surface](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/reference/index.html#predict-a-surface) and check where it applies | `predict_surface()`, `area_of_applicability()` | [Fitting and checking models](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/models.html) |
| 11. Report | `ensure_stable_poly_id()`, `sf::st_write()` | [Exporting and reporting results](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/reporting.html) |

## Where to go next

The [articles](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/index.html), in reading order:

| Article | What it covers | In R |
|---|---|---|
| [Get started](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/getting-started.html) | Take a layer of points to cells with standard errors, a score from spatial cross-validation and a map that marks where its predictions apply. | `vignette("getting-started")` |
| [Choosing a resolution](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/resolution.html) | Decide how many cells the data support, and pass that count to the tessellation. | `vignette("resolution")` |
| [Building cells and summarising them](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/cells.html) | Draw the cells, put each observation in one, and report each cell's value with the right standard error. | `vignette("cells")` |
| [Spatial cross-validation](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/spatial-cross-validation.html) | Choose folds whose score matches the map you will make, size the blocks, and read every part of the result. | `vignette("spatial-cross-validation")` |
| [Fitting and checking models](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/models.html) | Pick a backend or write your own, compare backends on the same folds, check the residuals, and map where the predictions apply. | `vignette("models")` |
| [Exporting and reporting results](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/reporting.html) | Write the cells to a file others can join to, and report the numbers that say how far a cell value or a map can be trusted. | `vignette("reporting")` |
| [Worked example: North Carolina](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/spatialkit_nc_demo.html) | The pipeline on a simulated field over North Carolina, comparing four tessellations, two fold schemes and two backends at cell counts set by hand. | `vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo")` |
| [Troubleshooting and performance](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/troubleshooting.html) | The errors and warnings you are most likely to meet, what each means, and how to handle large layers, parallel folds, caches and the log. | `vignette("troubleshooting")` |
| [Terms used on these pages](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/articles/glossary.html) | Short definitions of the terms the articles and help pages use. | `vignette("glossary")` |

The numbered scripts in `system.file("scripts", package = "spatialkit")` run
each step on a simulated field; Get started lists them. Report a bug or ask a
question on the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/issues); the
[contributing guide](https://github.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md)
says what to include.

## Citation

```r
citation("spatialkit")
```

This prints the package entry and the papers behind the methods spatialkit
implements. Cite the paper as well as the package if you rely on
`area_of_applicability()` (Meyer and Pebesma 2021),
`make_folds(method = "nndm")` (Milà et al. 2022) or
`make_folds(method = "knndm")` (Linnenbrink et al. 2024). Do the same for
the model backends you use: the Hilbert space approximation in
`fit_bayesian_spatial_model()` (Riutort-Mayol et al. 2023), permutation
importance in `fit_rf_model()` (Strobl et al. 2007), coordinates as
predictors and blocked validation in `fit_rf_model()` and `cv_rf()` (Meyer et
al. 2019), and GWR, whose kernels and diagnostics follow `GWmodel` (Lu et al.
2014).
